098.subtitle: Ḍākinī at the throat, three-eyed and armed

commentary.meaning: This is where the hymn goes inside the body. For the next thirty-odd names it will move through the wheels of the subtle anatomy, and at each one it names the presiding goddess and describes her: her seat, her colour, her eyes, her weapons, her attendants, the bodily tissue she governs and the food she likes. The pattern established here is repeated almost point for point six more times, so it is worth learning as a template. The first name gives the location, the throat wheel called viśuddhi, purification. Then the colour, a light red. Then three eyes, which is Śiva's mark and not an ordinary goddess's. Then the weapons, headed by the skull-topped staff of the cremation-ground ascetics. Then, oddly, a count of faces: she has one. That last item looks like a throwaway until you notice what follows. The goddess of the next wheel has two faces, the one after that three, and so on down to six at the brow. The single face named here is the first term of a series that will run the length of the section.
commentary.history:
The six wheels are stations on the central channel that runs from the base of the trunk to the crown, each pictured as a lotus with a fixed number of petals, a seed-syllable, an element, a presiding god and goddess, and a set of attendant powers seated on the petals. The scheme in the form best known today was systematised late — the Ṣaṭcakranirūpaṇa, a sixteenth-century chapter that Arthur Avalon translated as The Serpent Power, is the text most people are actually quoting when they describe the cakras — but its components are much older and the tantras vary considerably in the details. This hymn's version is one such variant, and readers who come to it from a yoga manual will find the correspondences do not always match.

The order is the first surprise. The hymn does not start at the base and climb. It starts at the throat, works downward through the heart, the navel, the genitals and the base, and only then jumps to the brow and the crown. Commentators account for this in different ways and there is no settled explanation; what can be said is that the descent follows a coherent sequence of bodily tissues, from the skin inward to the marrow, and that this ordering by tissue rather than by ascent gives the section its logic.

Viśuddhi is vi plus śuddhi, thorough cleansing, from the root śudh. Its element is space, its lotus has sixteen petals bearing the sixteen vowels, and it sits at the base of the throat. The association of the throat with purification has an obvious mythological anchor. When the gods and the antigods churned the ocean of milk for the draught of immortality, what came up first was not the nectar but a poison, halāhala, dense enough to end the world. Śiva drank it and held it in his throat, which turned dark and gave him the name Nīlakaṇṭha, the blue-throated. He neither swallowed it nor spat it out. The wheel of purification is placed exactly where that happened, and the point is not that impurity is removed but that it is held and neutralised at the passage.

The goddess who holds the wheel is Ḍākinī. The ḍākinī in earlier literature is a fearsome female spirit of the cremation ground, an attendant of Kālī, and in Buddhist tantra the word names a whole class of enlightened female figures. Here she has been drawn into the Śrīvidyā body-scheme and made an aspect of the central goddess herself, which is what allows the hymn to name her among the thousand. She is three-eyed, and three eyes are the standard mark of Śiva; the tradition reads them as sun, moon and fire, the two lights that measure time and the one that consumes it. The third eye is also the weapon: when Kāma shot his flower-arrow at Śiva to break his meditation and turn him toward Pārvatī, Śiva opened the middle eye and burned him to ash on the spot, after which Kāma was known as Ananga, the bodiless — a story this hymn returns to elsewhere, and one that makes the third eye an instrument of destruction rather than of insight alone.

The khaṭvāṅga is a club made from the leg of a bedstead with a skull fixed at the top, and it belongs to a specific religious world. It is the emblem of the Kāpālikas, the skull-bearing ascetics, and behind it stands the story of Śiva striking off the fifth head of Brahmā and having to wander as a beggar with the skull stuck to his hand until the guilt of brahmanicide was worked off. The staff is the penance made into an ornament. Its appearance in the hands of the throat-goddess of a hymn otherwise full of jewels and flowers is a deliberate importation of the cremation ground into the body. The compound ends in ādi, and the rest, which is the text's own admission that the full list of what she carries is not fixed; the iconographic manuals give her different numbers of arms and different implements.

One face, finally, and the number is meant literally. The count rises by one at each wheel as the hymn descends, reaching six at the brow. Whatever else the series does, it makes the section impossible to recite out of order once you have heard it: the faces count you down the body.
commentary.practice:
The line-break in the first line falls inside a word, and the printed text shows it with a doubled avagraha: viśuddhicakranilayā''raktavarṇā. Two separate names have run together in sandhi. Nilayā ends in long ā and āraktavarṇā begins with long ā, and two long ās give a single long ā, so what you actually say is one continuous vowel — nilayāraktavarṇā — with nothing audible at the join. The double mark is an editorial convention telling you that a long ā has been absorbed, not an instruction to stop. Reciters who pause there produce a word that does not exist.

Because the names have fused, this is a place where people lose count. It is one word in the mouth and two names in the archanā, where they separate cleanly again as viśuddhicakranilayāyai namaḥ and āraktavarṇāyai namaḥ.

The consonants to work on are the retroflexes and the aspirates in khaṭvāṅgādipraharaṇā, which is the hardest word in the verse. It opens with kha, a single aspirated guttural — k with a following puff, not k plus h as two sounds. Then ṭvā, with the tongue curled back to the roof of the mouth for ṭ before the v. Then ṅgā, where ṅ is the nasal made at the same place as g, the sound English writes in singer; hold the nasal, then release the g cleanly. Then a long stretch of light syllables, di-pra-ha-ra, before the retroflex ṇā at the end. The word rewards being broken into its pieces — khaṭvā, aṅga, ādi, praharaṇa — and rebuilt.

In āraktavarṇā, note that the ṇ is retroflex because of the r that precedes it. This is a regular rule of Sanskrit and you will meet it constantly: an r or ṛ earlier in a word turns a following n into ṇ under the right conditions. Once you hear varṇā correctly you will hear praharaṇā correctly too, and both keep the tongue curled where careless recitation flattens them to dental n.

Trilocanā is easier than it looks. The tri is t followed by r, not the English tr of tree, which is made much further back; keep the t at the teeth. The o in locanā is always long in Sanskrit — there is no short o — so lo gets full value.

Vadanaikasamanvitā hides a join: vadana plus eka gives vadanaika, because a short a followed by e produces ai. Knowing this makes the word mean something instead of being a string of syllables, and it also fixes the diphthong, which is a full-length vowel, not a glide.

What the verse asks of the reciter is a shift of attention. Up to this point the hymn has described a goddess seated on a throne somewhere else. From here it describes the inside of the body of the person chanting. The traditional way of taking the section is to let the attention rest at the named place as the name is said — here, the hollow at the base of the throat, where the voice is being made. There is a plain physical sense to that: this is the one wheel you can feel working while you recite.

crossReferences.iast: viśuddhau te śuddhasphaṭikaviśadaṃ vyomajanakaṃ śivaṃ seve devīmapi śivasamānavyavasitām | yayoḥ kāntyā yāntyāḥ śaśikiraṇasārūpyasaraṇeḥ vidhūtāntardhvāntā vilasati cakorīva jagatī ||
crossReferences.translation: In your wheel of purification I serve Śiva, clear as pure crystal, the begetter of space, and the Goddess too, whose resolve is equal to his; by the radiance going out from them both, which travels in the likeness of moonbeams, the world shakes off its inward darkness and shines like the cakorī bird.
crossReferences.relevance: The Saundaryalaharī works through the same wheels in its own order, and this is its verse on viśuddhi. Note vyomajanaka, the begetter of space — the element assigned to this wheel — and note that the deity here is a pair rather than a single goddess, which is a real difference from the sahasranāma's treatment and a good illustration of how much the descriptions vary between texts.

crossReferences.iast: anādimadhyāntam anantavīryam anantabāhuṃ śaśisūryanetram | paśyāmi tvāṃ dīptahutāśavaktraṃ svatejasā viśvam idaṃ tapantam ||
crossReferences.translation: Without beginning, middle or end, of boundless power, with numberless arms, having the moon and the sun for eyes — so I see you, your mouth a blazing sacrificial fire, scorching this whole universe with your own heat.
crossReferences.relevance: The standard reading of the three eyes assigns them to the moon, the sun and fire, and Arjuna's vision names all three in a single line. It is also a useful check on how such descriptions work: the numberless arms and the two luminary eyes are not meant to be assembled into a picture that could be drawn.

references.title: The Serpent Power: The Ṣaṭ-cakra-nirūpaṇa and Pādukā-pañcaka
references.author: Arthur Avalon (Sir John Woodroffe), 1919
references.note: Still the indispensable book on the wheels, and the source, directly or at several removes, of nearly every English account of them. Read the translated text itself rather than Avalon's long introduction, and read it knowing that it is one tantra's system and not the system — the differences from this hymn's version are instructive.

references.title: The Kāpālikas and Kālāmukhas: Two Lost Śaivite Sects
references.author: David N. Lorenzen (University of California Press, 1972; 2nd ed. Motilal Banarsidass)
references.note: The scholarly account of the skull-bearing ascetics, their penance, and the literary evidence for what they actually did. This is where to go to understand why a khaṭvāṅga in a goddess's hand is a specific claim about lineage and not a generic fierce attribute.

references.title: Elements of Hindu Iconography
references.author: T. A. Gopinatha Rao (Madras, 1914–16; repr. Motilal Banarsidass)
references.note: Four volumes of patient description of what images hold and why, drawn from the śilpa texts and from the sculpture itself. Useful here for the khaṭvāṅga and for the point that the ādi at the end of the compound is doing real work: the manuals genuinely disagree about the rest of the weapons.

references.title: Saundaryalaharī (Devanagari with Roman transliteration)
references.author: Śṛṅgeri Śāradā Pīṭham
references.note: Verses 34 to 41 are that poem's tour of the wheels, and reading the whole run of eight beside this section of the hymn is the fastest way to see both what the two texts share and where they part company.
